claims.text: The starting eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical microstructure composed of dual-phase lamellar colonies.
The untreated alloy has limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittle behavior.
Dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries generate localized stress concentrations in the untreated alloy.
The localized stress concentrations caused by dislocation pile-ups lead to microcracking and eventual brittle failure.
A targeted secondary aging treatment can induce fine nanoscale secondary-phase precipitates in the alloy.
The aging treatment can make the precipitates nucleate selectively at lamellar-colony boundaries or interfaces.
The boundary precipitates will be mechanically ductile.
Appropriate aging temperature and time can produce nanoscale precipitates without coarsening the existing phases.
The proposed aging treatment can preserve overall phase stability while confining precipitation to colony boundaries.
The nanoscale boundary precipitates will absorb or deflect dislocations and provide alternate pathways for dislocation motion.
Absorption or deflection of dislocations by the precipitates will reduce dislocation pile-ups at lamellar interfaces.
Reducing dislocation pile-ups will alleviate local stress concentrations.
Reduced local stress concentrations will delay or inhibit microcrack nucleation.
The modified boundary structure will produce more homogeneous and controlled plastic deformation.
The treated alloy will have significantly greater room-temperature tensile ductility than the untreated alloy.
The treated alloy will maintain or increase tensile strength relative to the untreated alloy.
Precipitates will reinforce the lamellar structure and thereby maintain or increase strength.
Excessive precipitate coarsening could compromise the fine eutectic-colony microstructure or alter the overall phase balance.
The proposed benefits are intended for room-temperature tensile deformation and may not extend to high-temperature operation.

contradictions.description: The intervention is described as a thermal aging treatment requiring selection of temperature and time, but the conditions state that the treatment itself is performed at room-temperature tensile-testing conditions. This appears to conflate the aging conditions with the subsequent mechanical-test conditions.
